---
title: "Peak detection in count data"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE
)
lgr::get_logger("mlr3")$set_threshold("warn")
```

This case study detects peaks in simulated count data. Every sequence is background noise, and every other one also has a burst of high counts. The labels mark where peaks start and end, and where there are none.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3changepoint)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Simulated counts

Each sequence has 500 Poisson counts. The background rate is drawn between 1 and 5, so the right penalty differs between sequences. Odd sequences have a peak of 41 to 81 positions at six times the background rate, labelled with `peakStart` and `peakEnd` regions around its edges and `noPeaks` regions on either side. Even sequences are labelled `noPeaks` from end to end.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
n_seq = 40L
n_data = 500L
counts = vector("list", n_seq)
label = vector("list", n_seq)
for (i in seq_len(n_seq)) {
  rate = runif(1L, 1, 5)
  y = rpois(n_data, rate)
  if (i %% 2L == 1L) {
    peak_start = sample(150:300, 1L)
    peak_end = peak_start + sample(40:80, 1L)
    y[peak_start:peak_end] = rpois(peak_end - peak_start + 1L, 6 * rate)
    label[[i]] = data.table(
      start = c(1, peak_start - 10, peak_end - 10, peak_end + 30),
      end = c(peak_start - 30, peak_start + 10, peak_end + 10, n_data),
      label = c("noPeaks", "peakStart", "peakEnd", "noPeaks")
    )
  } else {
    label[[i]] = data.table(start = 1, end = n_data, label = "noPeaks")
  }
  counts[[i]] = y
}
task = TaskCpt$new(
  id = "peaks", backend = data.table(counts = counts, label = label),
  target = "label", sequence = "counts", label_type = "peak"
)
```

The first four sequences show both kinds.

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Four panels of counts. Odd panels have a burst of high counts with shaded peakStart and peakEnd regions at its edges and noPeaks regions on either side. Even panels are flat with one noPeaks region."}
autoplot(task$clone()$filter(1:4))
```

## Train and test

`partition()` holds out 30% of the sequences for testing. `Kmax = 3` allows up to three peaks per sequence, more than the labels need.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sets = partition(task, ratio = 0.7)
learner = lrn("changepoint.intregrcv", Kmax = 3L)
learner$train(task, row_ids = sets$train)
prediction = learner$predict(task, row_ids = sets$test)
prediction$score(msrs(c("changepoint.label_error", "changepoint.auc")), task = task)
```

The scores are on the twelve test sequences, which the learner did not see.

## Decoded peaks

For peak tasks, `autoplot()` draws each predicted peak as a horizontal segment at its mean count. Here it shows four test sequences.

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Four test sequences of counts with their labelled regions and horizontal segments at the predicted peaks."}
autoplot(learner$predict(task, row_ids = head(sets$test, 4L)), task = task)
```

A segment that starts inside the `peakStart` region and ends inside the `peakEnd` region gets both labels right.
